name: rvv-bench (RISC-V Vector hand-written assembly kernels)
baseline: the board's libc strlen/memcpy/memset (libc implementation not named on the result pages, likely glibc on riscv64), plus clang-18 -O3 auto-vectorized scalar C for the same function (scalar_autovec rows), plus musl C versions
workload: bench/*.S RVV assembly kernels (strlen, memcpy, memset, utf8_count, mergelines, base64 encode, chacha20, poly1305, histogram, transposes) timed in bytes/cycle over buffer sizes from 1 byte to about 128 MB on a SpacemiT X60 (Banana Pi BPI-F3) board
claimed_speedup: SpacemiT X60 results in rvv-bench-results (data in bytes/cycle): strlen at 13255 B libc 1.3979 vs rvv_page_aligned_m8 5.6814 (4.1x, derived from page data); at 1309 B libc 1.1623 vs rvv_page_aligned_m4 2.7426; at 131936144 B libc 0.366 vs rvv_page_aligned_m8 1.002 (2.7x derived) while the plain fault-only-first rvv_m8 variant is 0.327 (slower than libc). Other pages in the same result set (memcpy.html, memset.html, utf8_count.html): memcpy at 3332 B libc 1.7927 vs rvv_m8 4.7897 (2.7x derived), at 64059557 B libc 1.4632 vs rvv_align_dest_m8 1.7162 (1.2x derived); memset at 3332 B libc 9.6137 vs rvv_tail_m2 11.4376 and about 4.54 for every variant at 127 MB; utf8_count at 3332 B scalar_autovec 0.7124 vs rvv_vlmax_m8 7.4209 (10x derived). Companion article articles/vector-utf.html: RVV UTF-8 to UTF-16 conversion 'on average 3 to 5 times' faster than scalar on real hardware, 8x for C908 and X60 and 11x for C920 on the all-ASCII case.
compiler_and_flags: config.mk default: cc -march=rv64gcv -O3 (clang 18 named for the scalar_autovec rows on the result page); freestanding option clang --target=riscv64 -march=rv64gcv_zba_zbb_zbs -O3 -nostdlib -fno-builtin
hardware: SpacemiT X60 (8 cores at 1.6 GHz, VLEN 256) in a Banana Pi BPI-F3; the results repo also holds boards such as Kendryte K230 (C908), Milk-V Pioneer (C920), SiFive P870, Tenstorrent X280
tradeoffs: Kernels target RISC-V with the V extension (RVV 1.0); per-LMUL variants (m1/m2/m4/m8) win on different cores, so the best variant is hardware specific and permutation-heavy kernels (vrgather, vcompress) do not scale uniformly across vendors. Several kernels are RVV intrinsics in the C reference and assembly in the .S file.
caveats: The README of the bench repo carries no numbers; numbers come from per-board HTML pages in the separate rvv-bench-results repo (the github.io rendering is blocked here, so the embedded plot data in the raw HTML files was parsed and the figures above are read from it). Gains shrink or vanish once the buffer is DRAM bound (memcpy 64 MB: 1.46 vs 1.72 B/cycle; memset 127 MB: every variant 4.54 B/cycle) and some variants lose (strlen plain rvv_m8 0.327 vs libc 0.366 B/cycle at 132 MB). The libc baseline is whatever libc the board ships (not named on the result pages), so the margin may reflect a weak generic baseline rather than a tuned scalar one. Compiler version for the build of each result is not pinned beyond the clang18 label; several boards are single-sample runs. Multiple kernels in one suite: the entry is a shootout of kernels, not one library.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts): camel-cdr/rvv-bench opened on github.com, then rvv-bench-results spacemit_x60/{strlen,memcpy,memset,utf8_count}.html and articles/vector-utf.html fetched via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: pqm4 (Cortex-M4 assembly post-quantum implementations)
baseline: PQClean 'clean' portable C implementation of the same scheme (ref for FN-DSA), compiled with arm-none-eabi-gcc 11.3.1 at pqm4's speed optimisation setting
workload: Cycle counts (min/avg/max over 10-1000 executions) for ML-KEM-512/768/1024 keygen/encaps/decaps, ML-DSA-44/65/87 keygen/sign/verify and FN-DSA on an STM32F4 Discovery board at 24 MHz, per implementation variant (clean/ref, opt, m4f, m4fspeed, m4fstack)
claimed_speedup: benchmarks.md averages in cycles, clean vs m4fspeed/m4f: ml-kem-768 keygen 988,722 vs 642,096, encaps 1,138,225 vs 658,754, decaps 1,387,984 vs 707,827 (1.5x, 1.7x, 2.0x derived from page data); ml-kem-1024 keygen 1,536,343 vs 1,018,976; ml-dsa-65 sign 12,359,056 vs 6,193,171 (2.0x derived) and verify 3,377,305 vs 2,415,944 (1.4x derived); fndsa_provisional-1024 sign 107,512,779 (ref) vs 48,321,135 (m4f) (2.2x derived).
compiler_and_flags: arm-none-eabi-gcc (Arm GNU Toolchain 11.3.Rel1) 11.3.1 20220712; pqm4 --opt speed (default); exact -O level lives in the build makefiles and was not opened
hardware: STM32F4 Discovery (Cortex-M4F), cycle counts taken at 24 MHz to avoid flash wait states
license: Apache-2.0 AND CC0-1.0 (repo-level); each implementation directory carries its own licence file
tradeoffs: Cortex-M4-only assembly (NTT, Keccak, field arithmetic); the m4fstack variants trade 1.2-3x speed for tiny stack use (ml-dsa-65 sign 24,421,526 cycles for m4fstack vs 6,193,171 for m4f). Code is not portable to other ARM cores or x86.
caveats: The m4 variants contain C-level and algorithmic changes as well as assembly, so the margin is not purely assembly versus compiler. The repository states pqm4 is no longer maintained and will be archived read-only in or after January 2027 (the PQ Code Package, mlkem-native and mldsa-native, is the suggested successor). Per-implementation licences differ, check each directory. The README itself notes the assembly SHA-512 gave a negligible speedup over C with arm-none-eabi-gcc 8.3.0 but was significantly faster with gcc 5.4.1.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts): pqm4 benchmarks.md as a cross-implementation PQC speed shootout on Cortex-M4; opened github.com/mupq/pqm4 README and benchmarks.md (raw.githubusercontent.com)

name: pospop (positional population count, Go assembly + C)
language: Go (assembly kernels), with a C version in src.c
baseline: the repo's own portable pure-Go kernels (generic8/16/32/64 positional popcount), compiled by Go 1.16
workload: positional population count (per-bit-position counts) over a 100 kB buffer, GB/s per kernel
claimed_speedup: README table (100 kB buffer, GB/s): amd64 avx512 82.1, avx2 34.8, sse2 16.0 versus generic8 1.02, generic16 1.71, generic32 2.66, generic64 3.43 (avx512 is 24x the best generic64 and 80x generic8; avx2 10x and 34x; derived from page data); arm64 neon 36.9 versus generic8 1.68 and generic64 6.56 (5.6x to 22x derived); 386 avx2 31.6 versus generic8 0.297.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.16 for all rows; all amd64 kernels are compiled in regardless of GOAMD64 (v1/v3/v4 correspond to sse2/avx2/avx512 rows)
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6138 @ 2.00 GHz (amd64 and 386); Apple M1 (arm64); ARM Cortex-A72 r0p3 on Raspberry Pi 4B (arm)
tradeoffs: AVX2/AVX-512/NEON/SSE2 kernels written as Go assembly (countavx2_amd64.s, countavx512_amd64.s, countneon_arm64.s); the arm32 build has no SIMD kernel. Specialised operation, not a general-purpose replacement for any standard library routine.
caveats: The baseline is the repository's own scalar Go code rather than a widely used external library; the README does not compare against the earlier Mula-Kurz-Lemire AVX2 popcount code or give cycles/byte. The README cites the peer-reviewed paper by Clausecker, Lemire and Schintke (Concurrency and Computation: Practice and Experience 2025) which was not opened here (blocked), so tier A rests on the README table and public benchmark code.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts): WebSearch snippet pointing at arXiv 2412.16370 'Faster Positional-Population Counts for AVX2, AVX-512, and ASIMD'; project found at github.com/clausecker/pospop

name: segmentio/asm (AVO-generated Go assembly)
baseline: the same package built with the purego tag (pure-Go fallback implementations, Go toolchain)
workload: README showcase benchmarks: ascii.EqualFoldString over 512-byte strings, bswap.Swap64, and qsort.Sort16 over 1,000,000 16-byte items
claimed_speedup: README benchstat (old purego vs new asm): EqualFoldString/0512 276 ns to 21 ns (-92.50%, 3.71 GB/s to 49.44 GB/s); Swap64 11.2 us to 0.9 us (-92.06%, 5.83 GB/s to 73.67 GB/s); Sort16/1000000 269 ms to 46 ms (-83.08%, 59.4 MB/s to 351.2 MB/s).
compiler_and_flags: Go version not stated; the Makefile benchcmp target runs go test -bench with -tags purego versus default, then benchstat
hardware: darwin/amd64, Intel Core i9-8950HK @ 2.90 GHz; n=5+5 samples
tradeoffs: amd64 assembly (qsort amd64 only, arm64 for some packages) with generic Go fallback elsewhere; purego build tag disables assembly; API is fixed-width-item oriented (bswap, qsort on fixed-size items, keyset, sortedset).
caveats: Only three showcase benchmarks, from one laptop (turbo-boost class CPU), compiler version unstated, and the README labels columns old/new without naming the baseline; the baseline identification (pure-Go build of the same package) comes from the Makefile benchcmp target. Not compared with Go standard-library functions such as strings.EqualFold or sort.Slice directly. Last commit is the November 2023 licence change.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts): WebSearch on Go assembly libraries with pure-Go vs asm benchmark tables; opened github.com/segmentio/asm, README and Makefile via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: minio/md5-simd (AVX2/AVX-512 multi-lane MD5 in Go assembly)
workload: BenchmarkParallel: aggregate MD5 throughput when many independent streams are hashed at once, per-write block size 32 KB to 8 MB, on a c5.xlarge
claimed_speedup: README benchcmp, crypto/md5 vs AVX512 (MB/s): 32 KB 2229.22 vs 11605.78 (5.21x); 1 MB 2233.56 vs 16941.95 (7.59x); 8 MB 2182.48 vs 17252.88 (7.91x). AVX2: 32 KB 7370.50 (3.31x), 4 MB 8993.61 (4.09x). Single-thread: BenchmarkCryptoMd5-4 687.66 MB/s, BenchmarkBlock8-4 4144.80 MB/s, BenchmarkBlock16-4 8228.88 MB/s.
compiler_and_flags: Go version and flags not stated; commands that produced the benchcmp inputs are not given
hardware: AWS EC2 c5.xlarge, Intel Xeon Platinum 8124M @ 3.0 GHz (AVX-512 capable)
tradeoffs: Does not speed up a single hash; it computes 8 (AVX2) or 16 (AVX-512) independent MD5 sums on one core, so it only helps servers that hash many streams concurrently (for example S3 ETag computation). The amd64 assembly uses VPGATHER and AVX-512 instructions; other architectures fall back to stdlib.
caveats: Headline 'up to 8x for AVX512 and 4x for AVX2' is rounded up from the table maxima of 7.91x and 4.09x. Hardware named but Go version, flags and benchmark commands are missing, so this is first-party partial methodology. Baseline is Go's crypto/md5, not OpenSSL or an assembly MD5 in C.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts): WebSearch on Go assembly libraries (minio/sha256-simd family); opened github.com/minio/md5-simd and commits page

name: klauspost/reedsolomon (Go Reed-Solomon with SSSE3/AVX2/AVX-512/GFNI/NEON assembly)
baseline: the library's own pure-Go Galois-field code path (Go column of the README table)
workload: erasure-coding encode of 1 MB shards using 32 threads, data+parity configurations 5+2, 8+8, 10+4 and 50+20
claimed_speedup: README encode table, Go vs AVX2 vs GFNI (MB/s): 5+2 40,690 vs 202,283 vs 241,747 (5.0x and 5.9x derived from page data); 8+8 14,244 vs 128,343 vs 271,680 (9.0x and 19.1x derived); 10+4 17,999 vs 152,673 vs 273,628; 50+20 3,520 vs 44,734 vs 47,706.
tradeoffs: Assembly paths exist for amd64 (SSSE3, AVX2, AVX-512, GFNI), arm64 NEON and ppc64le; everything else uses the pure-Go path. Table is aggregate across 32 threads, not per core.
caveats: README names no CPU model, Go version or run commands for the AMD64 table, and compares only to its own pure-Go path (no Intel ISA-L or Backblaze Java numbers). Included as an asm-versus-compiled-Go shootout, not a head-to-head with another library.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts): recall of Go assembly erasure-coding libraries; opened github.com/klauspost/reedsolomon and commits page

name: tinymembench (hand-written NEON/SSE2/AArch64 memcpy and memset kernels shootout)
language: C and assembly (ARM NEON, AArch64, x86 SSE2, MIPS-32)
baseline: the C copy loop built with the user's compiler flags, and the platform libc memcpy/memset ('standard memcpy', 'standard memset' rows)
workload: sequential memory copy and fill bandwidth over large buffers (MB/s), assembly variants such as SSE2 nontemporal copy, SSE2 fill, NEON LDP/STP copy, versus C copy and libc rows, on 60+ community-submitted machines listed on the project wiki
claimed_speedup: Wiki page for AMD Ryzen 9 5900X (2x16GB DDR4 3600): C copy 14480.0 MB/s, standard memcpy 26982.2, SSE2 nontemporal copy 27087.1 (1.9x over C copy, 1.00x over libc memcpy, derived from page data); standard memset 28594.4 vs SSE2 fill 44456.4 (1.55x, derived). Apple M1 page: C copy 18397.3, standard memcpy 29071.8, NEON LDP/STP copy pldl1keep 29088.1 (1.6x over C copy, parity with libc); standard memset 48748.7 vs NEON STP fill 48882.3 (parity). Tegra aarch64 board page: standard memcpy 3558.8 vs NEON LDP/STP copy pldl1keep (64 bytes step) 3884.0 (1.09x derived).
compiler_and_flags: not stated on the result pages; README build examples use CFLAGS="-O2 -mcpu=cortex-a9" make
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X with 2x16GB DDR4 3600 (primary row); other wiki pages cover Apple M1/M2, Intel Core i9-13900K, Raspberry Pi 1/2/4, Ryzen 7900X3D/9800X3D and many ARM SoC boards
stars_or_usage: 418 stars; results for about 60 devices on the wiki
tradeoffs: Assembly kernels are bandwidth-test loops for large aligned blocks, not drop-in memcpy replacements (no small-size or unaligned handling, no ifunc dispatch); nontemporal variants bypass cache and can hurt when the destination is reused.
caveats: Results are user-submitted wiki pages, one run each, with no compiler or flags recorded; on modern x86 and Apple M1 the best assembly copy only ties libc memcpy (the win is against the plain C copy loop and, for fill, against libc memset on Zen 3). Repository untouched since February 2017; version 0.4.9 header on all pages.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts): recall of memory-bandwidth shootouts with hand-written assembly kernels; opened github.com/ssvb/tinymembench, the wiki Home index and the AMD Ryzen 9 5900X, Apple M1 pages

name: nadavrot/memset_benchmark (assembly memset and memcpy, landed in folly)
language: Assembly (impl.S) with C reference implementations and benchmark tools
baseline: glibc memset/memcpy (measured both through the PLT and called directly), musl memset, and folly memcpy
workload: mixed-size benchmark with random buffer sizes 0 to 256 bytes and random offsets (pre-computed random values, nop call overhead subtracted) plus size sweeps 0-512 bytes; time per run, lower is better
claimed_speedup: README chart images (read from docs/memset_r.png and docs/memcpy_r.png; units unlabeled, lower is better): memset libc@plt 24344, libc 20172, asm_memset 14295 (1.4x over libc and 1.7x over libc@plt, derived from chart values); memcpy libc@plt 28285, libc 25263, folly 23969, asm_memcpy 21547 (1.17x over libc and 1.11x over folly, derived). README text: 'These implementations outperform the folly and glibc implementations.'
stars_or_usage: 344 stars; the memset implementation was adopted into facebook/folly (folly/memset.S) per the README
tradeoffs: x86-64 and AArch64 assembly tuned for small sizes (typical Chrome/Firefox call size distributions); drop-in via the repo's LD_PRELOAD proxy tool. No ifunc-style dispatch across microarchitectures.
caveats: Numbers exist only inside PNG charts (read from the images by eye); CPU, compiler and flags are not stated, so reproducibility cannot be checked. The repository root lists only docs, include, src, .gitignore, CMakeLists.txt and README.md and no LICENSE, LICENSE.txt or LICENSE.md could be fetched, so usability is marked reference (the folly port carries folly's Apache-2.0 licence). Repository last updated January 2022.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts): memset/memcpy shootout charts; opened github.com/nadavrot/memset_benchmark README and downloaded docs/*.png via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: CRYPTOGAMS (dot-asm/cryptogams, perlasm crypto kernels for x86_64, ARM, RISC-V, PPC, MIPS, s390x)
language: Perl-generated assembly (x86_64, ARMv4/v8, RISC-V, PPC, MIPS, SPARC, s390x, IA64, webasm)
baseline: gcc 4.8 compiled C (integer 'IALU' column) for the same ChaCha20 and Poly1305 algorithm; for Poly1305 the footnote says the comparison is against __int128 C code and gains over clang are about 50%
workload: cycles per byte out of large buffers for ChaCha20 (x86_64/chacha-x86_64.pl) and Poly1305 blocks (x86_64/poly1305-x86_64.pl) across Intel, AMD, VIA and Atom-class cores, with scalar integer, SSSE3, AVX, AVX2 and AVX-512 code paths
claimed_speedup: chacha-x86_64.pl header: Haswell 5.92 cpb scalar integer asm '+43%' versus gcc 4.8, then 1x SSSE3 5.20, 2x SSSE3 3.45, 4x SSSE3 2.42 and 8x AVX2 1.23 cpb; Skylake 5.87/+39% scalar, 1.19 cpb best vector; Ryzen 5.96/+50% scalar, 2.40 cpb 4x SSSE3; P4 9.48/+99%. poly1305-x86_64.pl header: Haswell 1.14 cpb integer asm '+175%' versus gcc 4.8, AVX2 0.65 cpb; Westmere 1.88/+120%; Ryzen 1.15/+200%. The header notes that against older gcc 3.x there is a '>2x improvement on most platforms'.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 4.8 (flags not stated); clang comparison only described in a footnote for Poly1305
hardware: Per-row CPUs in the header table: P4, Core2, Westmere, Sandy Bridge, Ivy Bridge, Haswell, Skylake-X, Cannon Lake, Rocket Lake, Silvermont, Knights Landing, Goldmont, Bulldozer, Ryzen, VIA Nano; timings measured with rdtsc at fixed clock
license: BSD-3-Clause OR GPL-2.0-or-later (CRYPTOGAMS licence text with GPL alternative)
stars_or_usage: 70 stars; the same generators feed OpenSSL's x86_64 and ARM assembly
tradeoffs: Per-architecture assembly generated by perl scripts and assembled with a 'flavour' argument; many code paths are specific to one ISA extension (AVX-512, IFMA), and the author says AVX-512 paths on Skylake-X are deliberately suppressed because they can slow the whole system. The README says pull requests are currently ignored and OpenSSL-common issues go through OpenSSL channels.
caveats: Numbers live in comment headers of each .pl file, not in a harness in the repo; the C reference and the compiler flags used for the gcc 4.8 comparison are not included, and gcc 4.8 is old (the Poly1305 note says clang gains are about 50%). The repository README itself makes no performance claims. Only the x86_64 ChaCha20 and Poly1305 headers were read for this entry; the arm/*-armv8.pl headers carry Cortex-X925 and Snapdragon X results.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts): github.com/topics/cryptography?l=assembly listing led to dot-asm/cryptogams; headers read from raw.githubusercontent.com x86_64/chacha-x86_64.pl and poly1305-x86_64.pl

name: ammarfaizi2/memcpy_benchmark (NASM AVX/AVX-512/rep movsb memcpy shootout)
baseline: libc memcpy as linked by cc
workload: one 128 MiB memcpy per iteration into a freshly malloc'd destination, repeated 10+ times, wall time in seconds (max/min/avg/total) for libc memcpy, memcpy_avx256, memcpy_avx512 and memcpy_movsb
claimed_speedup: result.txt: AMD A8-6410 libc memcpy avg 0.6221282 s vs AVX 0.4966940 s and rep movsb 0.4969657 s (1.25x, derived from page data); Intel Xeon Platinum 8269CY libc avg 0.3852886 s vs AVX 0.2986639 s (1.29x), AVX-512 0.3150474 s (1.22x), rep movsb 0.3333147 s (1.16x) (all ratios derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Makefile: cc -Wall -ggdb3 -fPIC -fpic -O3; nasm -felf64; compiler version not stated
hardware: AMD A8-6410 APU (2 GHz) and Intel Xeon Platinum 8269CY (2.5 GHz), CPU flags printed in result.txt; run with the performance governor and nice -n -20
tradeoffs: Kernels are only exercised for one very large copy; no small-size or unaligned handling is benchmarked; AVX-512 build is skipped on CPUs without it. Public-domain dedication, no patent grant.
caveats: The harness times a single 128 MiB copy into destination memory that was malloc'd but not touched before, so first-touch page faults and DRAM behaviour are part of every timing; the measured gap is therefore a large-copy, cold-destination result and not a general memcpy comparison. Only two CPUs recorded, one run set each, no repeated-session statistics. Absolute throughput implied (about 0.35-0.6 GB/s) is low, consistent with page-fault dominated timings.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts): github.com/topics/performance?l=assembly listing; opened repo README, result.txt, Makefile and memcpy_bench.c via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: oxsv (hand-written x86-64 assembly CSV toolkit)
language: x86-64 assembly (NASM) with a small C argument parser
baseline: xsv (Rust CSV toolkit) for the CLI commands; naive C loops for the SIMD scanner microbenchmark
workload: README benchmark on a 1 GB CSV with 6.27M rows and 18 columns: count, headers, head, select, search, frequency, index, stats, sort, fmt; plus a 16 MB buffer microbenchmark of the assembly byte scanner versus naive C
claimed_speedup: README table (oxsv vs xsv): count 0.17s vs 13.14s (76x), headers 0.002s vs 0.044s (22x), select 0.82s vs 19.27s (24x), search 1.31s vs 25.63s (20x), frequency 1.14s vs 29.17s (26x), index 1.11s vs 14.22s (13x), stats 12.97s vs 74.25s (5.7x), sort 2.15s vs 47.58s (22x), fmt 2.43s vs 37.26s (15x). Microbenchmark ASM vs naive C on 16 MB: count_byte 8.9 GB/s vs 3.3 GB/s (2.7x), find_byte 11.3 GB/s vs 2.3 GB/s (5.0x).
compiler_and_flags: C layer built with gcc and the NASM modules; flags and versions not stated in the README
hardware: WSL2 with DDR4-3200; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Linux x86-64 only, AVX2 delimiter scanning with CPUID dispatch, mmap input; quoted-field parsing is opt-in (-q), so default behaviour differs from xsv's CSV semantics.
caveats: Results above 50x (count 76x) come from a single WSL2 run with no CPU model, compiler flags or xsv version; the count comparison likely measures a newline/delimiter scan against xsv's full CSV record parse, so the workloads are not equivalent. Brand-new, unreviewed repository. Last commit date not read from a commits page. Cap at tier C per the implausible-speedup rule.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts): github.com/topics/avx2?l=assembly listing; opened github.com/rxxuzi/oxsv README

name: cespare/xxhash (Go XXH64 with amd64 and arm64 assembly)
language: Go (hand-written Go assembly for amd64 and arm64)
baseline: the same package built with the purego tag (pure-Go XXH64 implementation compiled by the Go toolchain)
workload: Sum64 over inputs of 4 B, 16 B, 100 B, 4 KB and 10 MB, GB/s, benchstat of go test -bench 'Sum64$' with and without -tags purego
claimed_speedup: README table (purego vs asm, GB/s): 4 B 1.3 vs 1.2 (asm slower); 16 B 2.9 vs 3.5; 100 B 6.9 vs 8.1; 4 KB 11.7 vs 16.7 (1.4x derived); 10 MB 12.0 vs 17.3 (1.4x derived).
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.19.2; go test -benchtime 500ms -count 15 -bench 'Sum64$' with and without -tags purego, compared with benchstat
tradeoffs: Assembly for gc on amd64 and arm64 only (excluded on appengine and with the purego tag); other platforms use the pure-Go code. Scalar XXH64, not XXH3, so it does not use SIMD.
caveats: The gain is modest (about 1.4x on large inputs) and negative on 4-byte inputs; the baseline is the package's own pure-Go path, not the C xxHash or another Go hash library. Numbers are first-party but fully reproducible from the two commands in the README.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts): recall of Go packages shipping hand-written assembly with purego comparison; opened github.com/cespare/xxhash README (raw.githubusercontent.com), xxhash_amd64.s and commits page

name: Constantine (Nim crypto stack with x86-64 inline-assembly field arithmetic)
language: Nim (C ABI; Go, Rust and C bindings), with x86-64 inline assembly (MULX/ADCX/ADOX)
baseline: the same finite-field arithmetic written in portable C/Nim with compiler add-with-carry intrinsics (GCC and Clang, no inline assembly)
workload: finite-field arithmetic for BLS12-381 (6 limbs) and the elliptic-curve and pairing operations built on it, benchmarked through the nimble bench_* tasks (bench_fp, bench_pairing_bls12_381, bench_ec_g1_msm_*)
claimed_speedup: README-PERFORMANCE.md: 'The speed improvement on finite field arithmetic is up 60% with MULX, ADCX, ADOX on BLS12-381 (6 limbs)'; summary list: 'missed opportunities on recent CPUs that support MULX/ADCX/ADOX (~60% faster than Clang)' and '2.4x perf ratio between using plain GCC vs GCC with inline assembly'; also 'GCC is up to 2x slower than Clang due to mishandling of carries'.
compiler_and_flags: CC=clang nimble bench_* with assembly on (default on x86-64); CTT_ASM=0 disables the assembly path; GCC 7 or Clang 14 minimum
hardware: no CPU named for the asm-versus-compiler statements; the multi-scalar-multiplication charts in the same file use an i9-9980XE (18 cores, 4.1 GHz all-core turbo)
tradeoffs: Inline assembly only on x86-64 (ARM planned); portable Nim/C fallback elsewhere. The assembly is also a constant-time requirement (to stop compilers turning branchless code into branches), not only a speed measure.
caveats: The asm-versus-compiler percentages are prose statements with no table, CPU, or run log for the 60% and 2.4x figures; the 2.4x is stated as plain GCC versus GCC with inline assembly, so a Clang build already closes much of the gap. The README does not compare against blst, mcl, gnark-crypto or other libraries.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts): recall of pairing-crypto libraries not yet catalogued (blst, mcl and Constantine were checked); opened github.com/mratsim/constantine, README-PERFORMANCE.md (raw.githubusercontent.com) and commits page
